## The Physics of Parallel Battery Equalization

When you connect two batteries in parallel, you are effectively merging their voltage rails into a single node. In an idealized circuit theory model, if both sources share identical internal resistance and perfect capacity, they would instantly settle at the average of their voltages. However, real-world lead-acid or lithium-ion chemistries deviate from this simplicity. The moment you bridge a fully charged cell (say, 12.8V) to a depleted one (say, 12.0V), current flows immediately to equalize the potential difference.

The core question is determining exactly how much current that low-charged battery will draw from its healthy counterpart during this equalization phase. The answer isn't a fixed number like "5 amps" or "10 amps"; it is a dynamic variable determined by three specific factors: the voltage differential, the internal resistance of both batteries, and the impedance of the cabling connecting them.

Ohm's Law governs this interaction. The instantaneous current ($I$) flowing from the high-voltage source to the low-voltage source can be approximated using the formula:

$$I = \frac{V_{high} - V_{low}}{R_{internal\_1} + R_{internal\_2} + R_{cable}}$$

In this equation, $V_{high}$ is the voltage of the fully charged battery, and $V_{low}$ is the voltage of the discharged one. The denominator represents the total resistance in the loop. Lead-acid batteries typically have internal resistances ranging from 0.001 to 0.02 ohms depending on their age and chemistry, while cabling adds its own variable based on gauge and length.

If you connect a healthy 12V battery directly to a dead one with thick cables (low $R_{cable}$), the initial surge can be substantial. A typical flooded lead-acid battery might have an internal resistance of roughly 0.01 ohms. If your cabling is also near 0.01 ohms, and you have a 0.8V difference between the cells, the theoretical short-circuit current could approach 60 to 80 amps instantly. In reality, batteries are not ideal voltage sources; they possess a limit on how fast they can accept or deliver charge without triggering internal heating or chemical damage.

This is where the concept of "equalization" becomes critical. You must distinguish between bulk charging and equalization. When you parallel-connect batteries with different states of charge, the healthy battery acts as a charger for the dead one. However, this current is unregulated. Unlike a smart charger that limits current to safe thresholds (e.g., 1C or C/10), a direct parallel connection allows the current to spike based purely on voltage headroom.

### Practical Implementation and Risks

From an engineering standpoint, blindly paralleling batteries of mismatched states of charge is often considered poor practice unless you are in a specific recovery scenario where you intend to force a recharge. The primary pitfall is thermal runaway or premature plating. If the low-charged battery is old or sulfated, its internal resistance may have increased significantly. While this limits the current draw according to Ohm's Law, it also means the battery will heat up rapidly under high current loads, potentially leading to gas generation (in lead-acid) or thermal stress in lithium variants.

Consider a scenario where you are building a redundant power system using two 12V batteries. If Battery A is at 13.0V and Battery B is at 12.0V, connecting them directly will force current into Battery B. Without a fuse or a dedicated battery management system (BMS), this could damage the interconnects or cause the healthy battery to discharge below its minimum threshold very quickly if it cannot sustain the load.

A safer approach in production environments involves using a diode OR-ing circuit or a dedicated balancer module before paralleling. This ensures that current only flows from the higher voltage source to the lower one without allowing backflow once voltages equalize, though this adds complexity and voltage drop. For simple parallel connections, always ensure your cabling is rated for the worst-case surge current calculated by the voltage differential divided by the minimum expected internal resistance.

### Monitoring the Process

If you must perform this equalization, monitoring the current is essential. You can insert a shunt resistor in series with the connection and measure the voltage drop to calculate real-time amperage using `I = V_shunt / R_shunt`. Alternatively, modern multimeters with clamp-on functions or dedicated battery analyzers can log this transient data.

Once the voltages convergeâtypically within minutes for small differentials or hours for larger onesâthe current will naturally taper off to near zero. At this point, the batteries are at a common equilibrium voltage. However, note that the "low" battery may not be fully charged even after equalization stops; it has simply caught up to the voltage of the donor. To bring the low battery back to full capacity, you must then disconnect them and apply a controlled charge from an external source to the now-equalized bank.

Attempting to run a load off this parallel combination during the equalization phase is ill-advised. The healthy battery will attempt to feed both the charging current required for the weak battery and the load simultaneously, potentially driving the voltage down so low that the weak battery never recovers, effectively creating a dead short scenario where the healthy battery depletes rapidly to sustain the weak one. Always let the system reach equilibrium before applying any significant external load.
